title: Come, I will tell you
hook: a list: no partners, kindness to parents, don't kill children for poverty, fair measure, keep promises (6:151–152)
tomorrow: My prayer, my life, my death

segments.voice: Yesterday: sabba, don't insult their gods. Your line was don't insult. Did you speak of someone's faith with respect? Today, an invitation, and a list. Day four hundred four.

At a family gathering, an elderly relative waves you over. Come here, sit, I want to tell you something. You lean in, expecting a story. Instead they count off on their fingers the few things that actually matter. Be good to your parents. Don't cheat anyone. Keep your word. It's not a lecture. It's what's left after a long life of finding out. Near the end of surah six, after a long argument about food rules and customs the surah rejects, the Prophet ﷺ is told to say one word to the people: come.
screen: `COME HERE, SIT.` → `COUNTED ON THE FINGERS.` → `ONE WORD: COME.`

segments.voice: Verse one-fifty-one, in Pickthall's words: “Say: Come, I will recite unto you that which your Lord hath made a sacred duty for you.” The Arabic word for come is ta'alaw. Lexicons connect it to a root about height, so the call has a sense of come up, rise to this. Then the list. Don't set up anything as a partner with Allah. Be good to your parents. Don't kill your children out of poverty: We provide for you and for them. Don't go near shameful deeds, open or hidden. Don't take a life Allah has made sacred, except by right. Verse one-fifty-two keeps going. Don't touch an orphan's property except to improve it, until they come of age. Give full measure and full weight, in fairness. When you speak, be just, even if it's about a relative. Keep the covenant of Allah. And verse one-fifty-three: this is My straight path, so follow it, and don't follow other paths that scatter you. Some readers count ten items here, and hear an echo of the ten commandments Jews and Christians keep; the Qur'an's list stands in its own words. An early companion, Abdullah ibn Mas'ud, is reported in Tirmidhi's collection to have said: whoever wants to read the testament of the Prophet ﷺ, with his seal on it, let them read these verses. And look at what's on it. Almost none of it is about ritual. It's about parents, children, orphans, scales, speech and promises. The sacred duty is mostly how you treat the people right in front of you.
screen: `TA'ALAW — COME UP, RISE TO THIS.` · `PARENTS, CHILDREN, ORPHANS.` · `FULL MEASURE, JUST SPEECH.` · `THE TESTAMENT, SEALED.` · then, large: `COME, I WILL RECITE.`

segments.voice: Sit, and count the list slowly on your fingers: no partners with Allah, parents, children, nothing shameful, life is sacred, orphans, fair measure, just speech, keep promises, the straight path. Don't rush. When you reach the end, go back and stop on the one that catches. Maybe it's a call to a parent. Maybe it's a promise half kept. Choose that one for today. The bell holds the time.
Come. Ta'alaw: the Qur'an's invitation in surah six to hear what Allah has made a sacred duty, counted out like a list on the fingers. Today's word.
Your line: come, I'll recite it. Today, keep one thing on the list, on purpose, and know which one it was. Day four hundred four.

screen: `DAY 404 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: MY PRAYER, MY LIFE, MY DEATH.`

howItsDone: Muslim teachers often present 6:151–153 as a summary of core duties, and some memorize them as a set; Ibn Mas'ud's remark about the Prophet's sealed testament is often quoted with them.

fork.setup: you're asked to sum up what your Lord made a sacred duty. where does surah six begin the list?
options: with no partners for Allah, then kindness to parents.
fork.reveal: the list opens with not associating anything with Allah, and right after it, being good to parents.

original.note: Arabic: come (said to a group); lexicons link it to a root about height.

trapdoor: what you thought: a list of rules.
what it means: an invitation to hear the sacred duties, most of them about how you treat people.
what a scholar hears: a report from Ibn Abbas counts 6:151–153 among the muhkam verses, clear and binding in every age; Ibn Mas'ud called them the Prophet's sealed testament (Tirmidhi).
recall: the covering of a broken oath
